title: 1492 and after
hook: Granada falls, and the Muslims of Spain are later forced to convert or leave

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Alhambra, the red palace whose walls repeat one sentence. Your line was: no victor but allah. After a win, who and what did you notice helping? Day nine hundred forty-four.

South of Granada there's a mountain pass with a name that is really a story: the sigh of the Moor. People tell that the sultan who handed Granada over, Abu Abdallah, whom the Spanish called Boabdil, rode out with his household, stopped at that pass, turned for one last look at the city and the red palace, and wept. Whether he wept there, nobody can say for certain. What came after his surrender is better documented, and it is harder to hear. Today: fourteen ninety-two, and after.
screen: `THE SIGH OF THE MOOR.` → `ONE LAST LOOK BACK.` → `WHAT CAME AFTER.`

segments.voice: Granada did not fall in a final battle. It was surrendered by treaty to Ferdinand and Isabella, the Catholic monarchs of Spain, and the treaty made promises. Muslims could keep their mosques, their faith, their law, their property. Those promises did not last. Before long the authorities were pressing Muslims to be baptized, and in time, across Spain, the choice became baptism or exile. Families who stayed, because home was home, were baptized, and they came to be called Moriscos. Some of them became sincere Christians. Others kept Islam in secret, praying behind closed doors, teaching children quietly. And they wrote. Some Moriscos wrote Spanish in Arabic letters, copying prayers, stories of the prophets, and rules of worship in a script their neighbors couldn't read. A language hiding inside another language, so that faith could survive in a kitchen. The suspicion never lifted. There were rebellions, crushed. And in the end the Moriscos as a whole, even those who were truly Christian, were expelled from Spain, crossing to North Africa and beyond. Their neighbors had been through it already. In the same year Granada surrendered, the Jews of Spain were ordered to convert or leave, and Jewish families left. Two communities, the same choice. This closes our walk through al-Andalus, and this ending belongs in the story too, beside the arches and the books. Remember the Moriscos.
screen: `SURRENDERED, WITH PROMISES.` · `BAPTISM OR EXILE.` · `SPANISH IN ARABIC LETTERS.` · `EXPELLED, AS THE JEWS HAD BEEN.` · then, large: `REMEMBER THE MORISCOS.`

segments.voice: The practice: pray for the displaced, or if you don't pray, hold them in mind. Settle, and breathe. Think of a family made to leave a home they loved, the Moriscos at a harbor, or people forced from their homes today, whose names you may have heard in the news. Picture one ordinary thing they had to leave behind: a door key, a kitchen, a tree in a yard. Stay with that one thing. If you pray, you can remember them in your prayer, in whatever words are already yours. If you don't, just keep them company in your attention. The bell holds the time.
Fourteen ninety-two and after. Granada surrendered with promises that broke, and the Muslims who stayed, the Moriscos, were forced to convert and, in the end, expelled. Today's word.
Your line: remember the moriscos. Today, learn the story of one group of people displaced from their home, past or present, and say their name aloud once. Day nine hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: The loss of al-Andalus and the expulsion of the Moriscos are remembered in Muslim histories, poetry and sermons; some families in North Africa trace their roots to the Moriscos.

fork.setup: you're a Muslim family in Spain after the surrender. the promises have broken, and the choice is baptism or exile. what did families like yours do?

original.note: Arabic: al-Andalus, the name Muslims gave the lands they ruled in Spain and Portugal.

trapdoor: what you thought: just a date in a history book.
what it means: the year Granada was surrendered, and the start of the end for the Muslims of Spain, forced to convert and later expelled.
what a scholar hears: the treaty of Granada and its broken terms, Morisco writing in Arabic script, and an expulsion that echoed the Jews' expulsion before it.
